title: A giant crayfish contest leads scientists to a growing mystery
summary:
It started with a little friendly bragging. Biologist Caitlin Bloomer pulled a huge crayfish from the mud during a survey in Kentucky. Its species is actually called the Crawzilla crawdad, and she was sure it was the biggest crayfish anyone had ever seen.

When she showed it to a colleague, he took one look and said, "No way, I've caught bigger," Bloomer recalled. Bloomer teaches at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

That challenge turned into a nationwide search. Bloomer asked biologists and museum curators across the country to check their collections for unusually large crayfish. The team used calipers, tools that measure objects very precisely, to compare preserved specimens. They found 20 extra-large crayfish from 18 different species. The results were published in the scientific journal Ecology.

Bloomer's Crawzilla made the top 20. "I'm super proud of it," she said.

The winner was a Tennessee bottlebrush crayfish kept at West Liberty University in West Virginia. It was collected in 2011, and its body measured 86.6 millimeters, about 3.4 inches, not counting its tail, claws and antennae. Professor Zackary Graham said its hard upper shell alone is about the length of a credit card.

The search also raised a scientific puzzle. The largest crayfish of many species all seemed to stop growing at about 80 millimeters. Yet some crayfish elsewhere, such as the Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish, grow much larger.

The researchers checked whether location, oxygen levels or habitat type could explain the size limit, but they found no clear pattern. Instead, the limit may come from the animals' own bodies. Their hard outer shells, called exoskeletons, or their muscles might set a physical limit on how big North American crayfish can grow.
why_it_matters: Learning what limits an animal's size helps scientists understand how bodies are built and how old museum collections can still answer new questions.

keywords.explanation: A biologist is a scientist who studies living things.
Curators are people who take care of and study the objects in a museum's collection.
Calipers are tools that measure the size of an object very precisely.
Specimens are samples of plants or animals kept so scientists can study them.
Exoskeletons are hard outer coverings that protect the bodies of animals like crayfish and insects.
A habitat is the natural place where an animal or plant lives.

background_read: Crayfish, also called crawdads, are freshwater animals related to lobsters and shrimp.
Like other animals with exoskeletons, a crayfish must shed its hard outer shell and grow a new one in order to get bigger.
Museums and universities keep preserved animal specimens so scientists can compare and measure them many years later.
Scientists studying maximum size look at things like where an animal lives and how its body is built to find out what limits its growth.

KEY EVENT: A nationwide search of museum and university collections
├─ WHO: Caitlin Bloomer of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and other biologists and curators
└─ HOW: Measuring preserved crayfish with calipers; results in the journal Ecology

EVIDENCE: Location, oxygen and habitat showed no clear pattern
